detail.abstract: With the escalating impacts of climate change driving population displacement worldwide, the need for robust policy frameworks to address the plight of climate refugees has become increasingly urgent. In this study, I examine the development of national policy concerning international climate refugees. Climate refugee status is not currently established in international law. However, evolving discourse on refugee determination and admissions systems (RDS) suggests that although climate change is not currently a legally admissible threat on its own, in the future it could be considered when reviewing refugee applications. This might be particularly in circumstances where climate change has worsened violent conflicts or posed significant threats to human security. In the absence of a specific legally binding international framework and the growing number of people displaced across borders due to climate events, some states have begun establishing policies to address forced climate migration as part of their national immigration systems. The effects of which could resonate as global best practices when formal international law and policy on climate refugees develop in the future. This is what I refer to as the Bubble-Up Effect, where national-level policies influence international norms, instead of the usual trickle-down (top-down) norm diffusion. The literature on the subject of Climate Refugees is still nascent, despite recent expansion in the global discourse. Additional comprehensive analyses of the diverse policy approaches being adopted by different nations and the underlying factors shaping their responses are still needed. Furthermore, relatively greater attention is to be placed on the role of political economy, and even environmental/ecological factors, in shaping policy agendas, as well as the perspectives and experiences of affected communities in both national and international policy formulation processes. To address these gaps, this study takes a mixed-methods approach, which combines qualitative policy analysis with case studies and is framed within a political economy perspective. Content analysis is utilized to scrutinize legal proceedings, policy documents, and national policy frameworks that were developed to tackle the issue of international climate refugees. Meanwhile, case studies on the US, Canada, Australia, European Union, and Non-signatory countries (to the 1948 Refugee Convention) provide insights into the contextual factors that shape national policy responses, including political dynamics, institutional capacities, and socioeconomic considerations. This analysis identifies common features, divergences, and emerging best practices that may be useful as international norms on the issue develop. This study contributes to the discourse on the local-to-global evolution of refugee determination systems (RDS) and policy norms that could provide legal status and inform admission protocols for international climate refugees in the near or distant future.

title: Search in Credence Goods Markets
affiliations: Stony Brook University and University of Tokyo

detail.title: Search in Credence Goods Markets
detail.abstract: We study consumer search in markets for horizontally differentiated expert services. A consumer faces a problem of unknown severity and consults experts for diagnosis and treatment. Because experts differ in match value, consumers search not only for honest recommendations but also for a better match. We show that an honest equilibrium can arise when search costs are sufficiently low, whereas in markets with homogeneous experts, any positive search cost eliminates honesty. Thus, horizontal differentiation provides a novel mechanism through which consumer search disciplines expert conduct. We also show that improving the search pool can unintentionally increase expert cheating.

title: GLP-1 Receptor Agonists as Novel Pharmacotherapy for Substance Use and Behavioral Addictions: Clinical Evidence, Mechanisms, and Public Health Implications

detail.title: GLP-1 Receptor Agonists as Novel Pharmacotherapy for Substance Use and Behavioral Addictions: Clinical Evidence, Mechanisms, and Public Health Implications

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None.
declarations.funderStatement: None.

detail.abstract: Background: Substance use disorders (SUDs) and behavioral addictions represent a global public health crisis, affecting millions and contributing to significant mortality, morbidity, and economic burden. Current pharmacotherapies are limited in number, efficacy, and adoption. Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs), approved for type 2 diabetes and obesity, have emerged as promising novel treatments for addictive disorders based on accumulating preclinical and clinical evidence. Objective: This comprehensive white paper synthesizes the latest clinical evidence (2023-2025) on GLP-1RAs for addiction treatment, examines underlying neurobiological mechanisms, evaluates comparative effectiveness across substance types, and discusses policy, economic, and implementation implications. Methods: Systematic review of peer-reviewed literature, including randomized controlled trials (RCTs), real-world observational studies, registry analyses, and preclinical research published through December 2025. Primary focus on semaglutide, liraglutide, dulaglutide, and exenatide.

title: Many Men, Many Minds: A Multi-Agent LLM Approach to Disagreement and Global Asset Pricing
affiliations: , Shandong University of Finance and Economics and PBCSF, Tsinghua University

detail.title: Many Men, Many Minds: A Multi-Agent LLM Approach to Disagreement and Global Asset Pricing
detail.abstract: We develop a novel multi-agent framework based on large language models (LLMs) to quantify investor disagreement in cryptocurrency markets. By deploying three distinct Gemini-1.5-Flash agents to process financial news, we decompose disagreement into within-group belief dispersion and cross-group stance polarization. We uncover a sharp contrast in how these two components are priced: within-group uncertainty fuels speculative trading and exerts downward price pressure, consistent with heightened risk aversion (an uncertainty premium), whereas cross-group polarization reduces liquidity and predicts higher subsequent returns, consistent with short-sale constraints and canonical disagreement-based pricing mechanism. Extending the analysis to 32 global equity markets, we show that cryptocurrency-based disagreement is a powerful leading indicator of international equity returns, with predictive power orthogonal to standard global macro-financial factors. Notably, we document geographic heterogeneity in transmission: developed markets are more sensitive to bearish disagreement, whereas emerging markets respond more strongly to bullish disagreement. Recursive out-of-sample forecasting and economic value tests further indicate economically meaningful annualized certainty-equivalent return gains, especially in developed markets, highlighting cryptocurrency disagreement as a novel state variable for global asset pricing.

title: New-Keynesian Inflation Control is Equilibrium Selection
affiliations: Hoover Institution

detail.title: New-Keynesian Inflation Control is Equilibrium Selection
detail.abstract: The standard New-Keynesian model is often misinterpreted to embody old-Keynesian intuition: Higher nominal interest rates raise real interest rates, which lower output and employment, and via the Phillips curve lower inflation. That's not how the equations work. The entire ability of the standard model to lower inflation with higher nominal interest rates comes from a coincident equilibrium-selection/fiscal shock, independent of the interest rate movement. With short-term debt, any lowering of inflation requires a fiscal tightening. Long-term debt and sufficiently persistent shocks can produce lower inflation with no change in fiscal policy. The central role of equilibrium selection is hidden by Taylor rules with AR(1) disturbances. Non-AR(1) Taylor rule disturbances produce the same path of interest rates, but different inflation. The choice of disturbance process is thus an independent equilibrium-selection choice. It is more revealing to characterize the model's dynamics by the path of interest rates and the initial equilibrium-selection shock, which are observable, unlike Taylor rule disturbances.

title: Does Authority Framing Increase Susceptibility to Misinformation? An Experimental Analysis of Truthfulness, Sharing, Vigilance, and Confidence

detail.title: Does Authority Framing Increase Susceptibility to Misinformation? An Experimental Analysis of Truthfulness, Sharing, Vigilance, and Confidence

detail.abstract: The accelerating dissemination of misinformation in the digital era poses a serious societal challenge. This thesis explores how subtle cues of authority influence people's susceptibility to misinformation. A 2x2 between-subjects design online experiment was conducted (n=173), where participants were randomly assigned to view short videos presenting true or false news-style statements framed either as authoritative (university podium) or neutral (no cues). After viewing the videos as part of the survey, participants rated their perceived truthfulness, willingness to share, epistemic vigilance, and confidence in judgment (on 5-point Likert scales). The results indicated that authoritative framing significantly increases willingness to share misinformation and reduces participants' epistemic vigilance. Interestingly, no effects were found on perceived truthfulness and confidence in their judgment. Furthermore, media literacy and familiarity with academia moderate these effects, acting as protective factors against misinformation. Practical implications for media literacy education and information platform design are discussed.

title: Fintech and Financial Inclusion in Emerging Economies: Evidence From Digital Payments, Mobile Banking, and Entrepreneurial Finance

detail.abstract: Financial inclusion remains a persistent challenge in emerging economies, where large segments of the population lack access to formal financial services. The rapid diffusion of financial technology (FinTech) has been widely promoted as a transformative solution capable of bridging institutional gaps, reducing transaction costs, and expanding access to financial services. This study investigates the impact of FinTech adoption on financial inclusion in emerging economies, with particular emphasis on digital payments, mobile banking, and FinTech-enabled entrepreneurial finance. Using panel data from selected emerging economies between 2015 and 2024, the study employs fixed-effects regression and instrumental variable techniques to examine the relationship between FinTech penetration and financial inclusion indicators. The findings indicate that FinTech adoption significantly improves access to financial services, increases usage of formal financial products, and enhances financial participation among micro-entrepreneurs and underserved populations. However, the results also reveal persistent digital divides related to income, education, and infrastructure quality. The study contributes to the literature by providing empirical evidence on the inclusionary potential of FinTech while highlighting policy trade-offs relevant for regulators and development institutions.

title: Conspicuous Inequality: Speculative Housing Booms and Property Crime in China
affiliations: Tsinghua University - School of Economics & Management, ,  and INSE at Peking University

detail.title: Conspicuous Inequality: Speculative Housing Booms and Property Crime in China
detail.abstract: This paper identifies the causal effect of housing speculation on crime by exploiting spillovers from house purchase restrictions (HPR) in major Chinese cities. These policies redirected speculative demand to nearby unregulated markets, triggering sharp and exogenous housing booms. Using newly constructed measures of criminal activity derived from large-scale text analysis of court judgments, we show that speculative housing booms increase property crime but not violent crime. The rise is concentrated in financially motivated offenses—larceny, fraud, and high-value robbery—and is committed primarily by socioeconomically vulnerable individuals and first-time offenders. Mechanism analyses reveal that housing booms widen wealth inequality and make affluence more visible through conspicuous consumption, raising both the expected returns to crime and the ease of targeting. Alternative explanations such as deprivation, social strain, migration, or weakened deterrence find no support. The results highlight a new social cost of housing speculation: by amplifying visible inequality, it erodes cohesion and fuels crime.

title: Energy Shortage and Stock Return Predictability

detail.title: Energy Shortage and Stock Return Predictability

detail.abstract: This paper investigates the time-series predictability of the energy shortage index (ESI) for equity risk premiums. Our empirical results show that ESI is significantly and negatively associated with future stock returns, both in-sample and out-of-sample, and consistently outperforms a comprehensive set of traditional competing predictors. We further document that the predictive power of the ESI strengthens as the forecast horizon extends and remains robust across both economic expansions and recessions. Importantly, this predictability is not limited to the U.S. market but extends to major international equity markets. Portfolio analysis confirms that integrating ESI into mean-variance frameworks generates economically meaningful utility gains for investors. Mechanism analyses suggest that the predictive efficacy of the ESI stem from both the cash-flow and discount-rate channels, as well as its significant links to investor behavior and macroeconomic fundamentals. Finally, the predictive power of ESI is robust across cross-sections and alternative evaluation specifications.

title: Forecasting Global Stock Market Volatility in an Uncertain World
affiliations: Hunan University - School of Finance and Statistics,  and Hunan University of Finance and Economics

detail.title: Forecasting Global Stock Market Volatility in an Uncertain World

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.

detail.abstract: This paper constructs a novel aggregated uncertainty indicator based on machine learning to forecast monthly stock market volatility of international equity markets. We find that, compared with existing uncertainty indices, the aggregated uncertainty indicator demonstrates superior in-sample and out-of-sample forecasting performance across a broad cross-section of international stock markets. Specifically, it exhibits particularly strong short-term predictive power in developed markets, while displaying more pronounced long-term forecasting ability in emerging markets. Moreover, the economic value analysis demonstrates that incorporating the aggregated uncertainty index into investment strategies significantly enhances economic utility of investors relative to benchmark models. We further identify that uncertainty affects stock market volatility primarily through the channels of investor behavior and macroeconomic fundamentals. Finally, a series of robustness checks confirm the stability and reliability of our findings. Overall, this study provides new insights for global investors and regulators in understanding and managing market risk under uncertainty.

title: Institutional Non-Response: An Unmeasured Patient Safety Risk in Modern Health Systems

detail.title: Institutional Non-Response: An Unmeasured Patient Safety Risk in Modern Health Systems

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None.
declarations.funderStatement: This work received no external funding.

detail.abstract:
Patient safety frameworks have historically emphasized the identification and analysis of discrete adverse events, clinical errors, and sentinel outcomes after harm has occurred. Although these approaches have improved transparency and accountability, they are poorly suited to detecting safety risks that develop through prolonged periods of institutional inaction. As health care delivery becomes increasingly digitized, asynchronous, and distributed across teams, patient harm is less likely to arise from single catastrophic failures than from unresolved delays embedded in routine system operations.

This Viewpoint introduces institutional non-response, the failure of a health care system to act on known clinical or safety-relevant information within timeframes necessary to preserve patient safety, as an underrecognized and unmeasured patient safety risk. Distinct from diagnostic uncertainty or clinical error, institutional non-response reflects system latency after information has already been identified, documented, and acknowledged. Drawing on safety science, systems theory, and health information technology literature, this article argues that delayed follow-up, stalled escalation pathways, and procedural acknowledgment without clinical resolution constitute measurable pre-harm safety hazards that frequently evade existing oversight mechanisms. Recognizing institutional non-response as a safety signal may enable earlier detection of unsafe trajectories using data that health systems already collect and strengthen alignment between patient safety measurement, governance, and patient protection.

title: ESG Investing and Corporate Performance in Emerging Markets

detail.title: ESG Investing and Corporate Performance in Emerging Markets

detail.abstract: Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) investing has emerged as a key driver of sustainable corporate practices and long-term financial performance. While ESG adoption is extensively studied in developed markets, evidence from emerging economies remains limited and inconclusive due to unique institutional, regulatory, and market conditions. This study investigates the relationship between ESG performance and corporate financial outcomes measured by return on assets (ROA), return on equity (ROE), and Tobin's Q in 500 publicly listed firms across 15 emerging markets over the period 2015-2024. Using panel data regression models, complemented by robustness checks and instrumental variable estimation to address endogeneity, the study examines the differential effects of environmental, social, and governance components on firm performance and explores the moderating role of institutional quality. The results indicate that higher ESG performance is positively associated with corporate financial outcomes, with governance practices exhibiting the strongest influence. Institutional quality further strengthens the ESG-performance link, highlighting the importance of supportive regulatory and governance environments. The study contributes to the literature by extending empirical evidence of ESGfinancial performance linkages to emerging markets and offers actionable insights for policymakers, investors, and corporate managers seeking to leverage ESG practices for competitive advantage and sustainable growth.

title: Behind the Façade of the National Executive Councils of Political Parties in Africa: What the Governments Ought to Do or Not to Do?
affiliations: Durban University of Technology and Durban University of Technology (DUT)

detail.title: Behind the Façade of the National Executive Councils of Political Parties in Africa: What the Governments Ought to Do or Not to Do?
detail.abstract: This paper explores the intricate dynamics behind the façade of National Executive Councils (NECs) within political parties in Africa, scrutinizing their role in shaping governance and democratic practices. Despite often being perceived as bastions of democracy, many NECs function under opaque mechanisms that can perpetuate authoritarianism and hinder genuine political participation. This study examines the structural and operational challenges faced by NECs, including issues of internal dissent, lack of transparency, and the influence of external actors. This systematic qualitative method aimed to explore the Behind the façade of the National Executive Councils of Political Parties in Africa. The methodology involved a structured approach gathering and analysing qualitative data from relevant online literature sources, and expert opinions. Selection of articles focused on peer-reviewed 51 articles from 1971 to 2015 that discussed Behind the façade of the National Executive Councils of Political Parties in Africa. Data was categorised as the Behind the façade of the National Executive Councils of Political Parties in Africa. This systematic approach aimed to provide insights into Behind the façade of the National Executive Councils of Political Parties in Africa. The findings emphasize the need for governments to reform political party structures through promoting internal democracy, enhancing transparency, and fostering inclusive participation. It argues against excessive government intervention, advocating for a regulatory framework that supports self-regulation and accountability. The study highlights the importance of reforming National Electoral Commissions (NECs) to strengthen democracy in Africa and calls for collaboration among governments, civil society, and political actors to ensure that parties represent the electorate effectively, enhancing democratic governance.

title: The Police State vs. The Welfare State
affiliations: Srinivas University

detail.title: The Police State vs. The Welfare State

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No financial relationship
declarations.ethicsApproval: No ethical conflicts
declarations.funderStatement: No external funding

detail.abstract: This article looks at the conflict between the police state and the welfare state, which are two different ways of running a country that affect the relationship between the state and its citizens. The police state puts more emphasis on spying, force, and social control to keep order, whereas the welfare state puts more emphasis on social protection, economic redistribution, and public services to improve well-being and social stability. The essay examines the equilibrium between security and social welfare maintained by states in reaction to inequality, economic crises, and perceived threats, utilising political theory, historical instances, and current policy discussions. It contends that excessive dependence on police techniques frequently signifies deteriorated welfare institutions and might intensify social exclusion, whereas resilient welfare systems may mitigate the necessity for coercive control. The study suggests that the long-term legitimacy and stability of modern states rely on establishing a fair equilibrium between security and social provision, rather than favouring repression over social investment.

title: Evaluating Structural Credit Risk Models for Default Prediction in the Chinese Market

detail.title: Evaluating Structural Credit Risk Models for Default Prediction in the Chinese Market

detail.abstract: Structural credit risk models are widely used in default prediction practice, yet their effectiveness in the Chinese market remains unclear. Using a comprehensive dataset of recent corporate debt default events, we find that classical structural models have substantially weaker predictive power in China than in international markets. A defining institutional feature is that financially distressed firms often receive support from governments or controlling shareholders. We incorporate this feature into an augmented structural model, which explicitly accounts for external support and delivers a marked improvement in default prediction accuracy.

title: Parallel Futures Deliberation: A Novel Framework for Consensus Building under Socio-Technical Uncertainty
affiliations: Sophia University, Research Institute for Humanity and Nature (RIHN), The University of Tokyo, National Institute of Advanced Industrial Science and Technology (AIST), National Institute of Advanced Industrial Science and Technology (AIST), National Institute for Environmental Studies and Research Institute for Humanity and Nature (RIHN)

detail.title: Parallel Futures Deliberation: A Novel Framework for Consensus Building under Socio-Technical Uncertainty

declarations.funderStatement: This study was supported by the Research Institute for Humanity and Nature (RIHN: a constituent member of NIHU) Project No. RIHN 14200156.

detail.abstract: The governance of emerging technologies is confounded by the "Collingridge Dilemma." "Upstream" public engagement, or Participatory Technology Assessment (pTA), was developed to address this, but faces persistent, interconnected challenges: deliberation often remains abstract, empowering expert dominance and intensifying value conflicts under high sociotechnical uncertainty. This paper introduces and evaluates a novel framework, "Parallel Futures Deliberation (PFD)," designed to address this syndrome. Tested in a workshop with citizens and experts on the sociotechnical uncertainty of nitrogen circularity, PFD creates a concrete and equitable environment by structuring a sophisticated and complementary division of labor. This structure resolves the problem of expert dominance and grounds the debate in tangible future worlds. The framework systematically generates value conflict from its initial scenario-based assumptions, and then channels that conflict into two distinct, productive outcomes: a substantive synthesis for disagreements over "means," and a procedural consensus for intractable conflicts over "ends." This study contributes a novel deliberative method that bridges the ambitions of Participatory TA (pTA) and Constructive TA (CTA), offering a new framework for understanding how structured processes can transform value conflict into tangible agreements.

title: Demographic Stagnation and Revitalization in Japan: A Structural Analysis of Fertility Determinants, Labor Market Dualism, and Policy Efficacy

detail.title: Demographic Stagnation and Revitalization in Japan: A Structural Analysis of Fertility Determinants, Labor Market Dualism, and Policy Efficacy

contentType.other: Economics Network, Social Insurance Network, and Sociology Network.

detail.abstract: Japan faces an existential demographic crisis, with the Total Fertility Rate (TFR) falling to a record low of 1.15 in 2024 and annual births dropping below 700,000 for the first time. This paper analyzes the structural determinants of this decline, arguing that the government's recent "unprecedented" measures, including a 3.6 trillion yen annual investment in child-rearing support, may be insufficient because they primarily address the cost of living rather than the root causes: labor market dualism and entrenched gender inequity. Specifically, the analysis identifies the "1.03 million yen wall" tax threshold as a barrier to female labor participation and highlights how the economic precarity of non-regular employment among men has led to a significant decline in marriage rates. Through a comparative analysis of pro-natalist policies in France, Sweden, Hungary, and Estonia, this research concludes that structural reforms-such as enforcing equal pay for equal work, abolishing spousal tax deductions, and mandating paternity leave-are necessary to reverse the "low fertility trap".

title: Convexity and Latent Status: Understanding the Evolution of Intergenerational Educational Mobility in Japan
affiliations: George Washington University - Department of Economics, Hitotsubashi University and World Bank - Development Research Group (DECRG)

detail.title: Convexity and Latent Status: Understanding the Evolution of Intergenerational Educational Mobility in Japan

declarations.declarationOfInterest: There are no personal or financial relationships to be declared.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not Applicable.
declarations.funderStatement: This research was not funded by any sources.

keywords: Nonlinear Latent Status Model of Mobility

detail.abstract: We study intergenerational educational mobility in Japan, with a focus on its evolution from the 1940s to the 1990s birth cohorts.  Japan is an excellent case study for understanding the role of changing economic conditions in shaping intergenerational mobility, from the war-ravaged 1940s to the miracle growth in the 1950s-1970s, to the deep and persistent recession in the 1980s-2000s. Based on the theoretical model of Becker et al (2018), we allow for the possibility that the educational mobility curve can be concave or convex. In addition to the standard bivariate models of educational mobility based on children's and parents' schooling, we implement the latent status model where multiple indicators of children's socioeconomic status are used in a way to minimize the attenuation bias arising from measurement error. We report the first estimates of a nonlinear (quadratic) latent status model of intergenerational mobility in the literature. Our empirical analysis uses data from two high-quality household surveys: Keio household panel survey (KHPS) and Japan household panel survey (JHPS). These surveys collected the relevant information for both coresident and nonresident parents of a respondent, thus alleviating the concern of sample truncation bias in the estimates. The evidence rejects the linear model, except for one case, and shows that the shape of the mobility curve changes substantially across cohorts. For the bivariate model, mobility curve is convex in all cohorts, except for the 1940s for which it is linear. The degree of convexity increases in the later cohorts, implying that the persistence in educational advantages of the children of college-educated parents became much stronger during the decades of deep recession. The evidence suggests that the standard linear model often leads to incorrect conclusions. The linear bivariate model suggests no significant differences in relative educational mobility for the children of war (1940s cohort) and the children of recession (1990s cohort), while the quadratic model suggests a dramatic change in the educational opportunities of low-educated and high-educated households. The latent status approach suggests that father's occupation is much more informative as a proxy for children's socioeconomic status compared to mother's education, suggesting a weak labor market screening role of education in parental generation. The estimates of quadratic latent status model suggest that the mobility curve was concave in the 1940s and 1950s, but became convex in the 1960s and following cohorts. This flip in the shape implies that the pattern of persistence at the two tails of distribution reversed in the later cohorts, with a stronger persistence in the educational advantages of the children at the top of socioeconomic distribution. However, the degree of convexity in latent status estimates in the later cohorts is substantially smaller (compared to the bivariate model), consistent with strong diminishing returns to fathers' occupation and mothers' education, partly offsetting the strong convexity found in the bivariate model with father's education as the sole marker of status.

title: Market Efficiency as an Equilibrium Outcome of Predictable Behavior
affiliations: Rice University

detail.title: Market Efficiency as an Equilibrium Outcome of Predictable Behavior
detail.abstract: This paper provides an equilibrium interpretation of market efficiency based on predictable, rule-based behavior rather than rational expectations. We model agents as following stable decision policies that map information into actions and need not be optimal or unbiased. When such behavior is predictable, it is in principle learnable and therefore constitutes a potential trading signal. We show that in competitive markets, any systematic predictability in excess returns conditional on publicly available information is endogenized into asset prices through arbitrage and capital reallocation, eliminating risk-adjusted excess returns except where standard constraints-such as risk-bearing capacity, information costs, or trading frictions-bind. Predictable behavior therefore does not imply mispricing; instead, it is the mechanism through which market efficiency is enforced in equilibrium. The framework reconciles evidence of behavioral regularities with the Efficient Market Hypothesis and provides a unifying interpretation of rational expectations, behavioral finance, and limits-to-arbitrage arguments.

title: On Animal Status: The Value of a Statistical Life Versus the Value of a Statistical Animal Life (For a Pig)
affiliations: Florida State University - College of Law and Western Kentucky University

detail.title: On Animal Status: The Value of a Statistical Life Versus the Value of a Statistical Animal Life (For a Pig)

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no affiliations or involvement in any organization or entity with any financial interest in the subject matter or materials discussed in this manuscript.

detail.abstract: In a variety of regulatory and policy contexts, cost-benefit analysis is used to evaluate the normative desirability of a regulation, program, or policy, and these analyses measure effects on humans. The welfare of animals is very rarely taken into account. Research has produced estimates of how much monetary value people place on the humane treatment of animals, mostly livestock, but a focus on the prevention of cruelty to animals is incomplete. This narrow focus ignores a variety of harms imposed on animals in a wide array of contexts, such as habitat loss, pollution, and climate change. We assert that this omission is inefficient and indefensible. As an initial step, we estimate the value of a statistical animal life of $63 to $81 for a domestic pig, alongside an estimate of the value of a statistical human life. While a developed literature exists for estimation of the latter, there has been no effort to estimate the former, and certainly no effort to compare the two. We make these estimates to: (i) provide a very early step in providing some empirical foundation for the ethical status of animals vis-à-vis human beings, and (ii) establish a numerical comparison for purposes of conducting cost-benefit analyses for actions affecting animals. A value of statistical animal life that takes approximately 1:500,000 of a value of statistical human life provides a meaningful scale when evaluating regulations and policies.

title: The Emotional Tension Index (ETI): An Event-Based Structural Framework

detail.title: The Emotional Tension Index (ETI): An Event-Based Structural Framework

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no personal, professional, or financial relationships that could be perceived as influencing the research presented in this paper.

detail.abstract: This paper formalizes the Emotional Tension Index (ETI), an event-based structural framework for representing emotional tension using externally observable events rather than introspective self-report. ETI separates accumulated tension volume (ETI-A) from the distributional structure of the same events across time and context (ETI-G), and defines a divergence term (ETI-D = |ETI-A − ETI-G|) to summarize mismatches between magnitude and organization. The framework specifies a minimal event taxonomy, field reconstruction conditions, and interpretable structural signatures (e.g., clustering, bottlenecks, and suppression zones) that may not be visible in scalar summaries. A concise studio-based illustration in embodied arts education shows how ETI can be implemented from routine learning events without clinical labeling. To close the loop from signal to response, the paper also specifies ASLTP (Affect–Surface–Label– Transform–Present), a five-step classroom protocol designed to support low-intensity, nonclinical tension diffusion within ordinary instruction. ETI is presented as a descriptive structural layer intended to complement, not replace, qualitative, psychological, or physiological approaches.

title: Going AI-native: Turning Technology into Measurable Customer Value
affiliations: Mindanao State University - Iligan Institute of Technology

detail.title: Going AI-native: Turning Technology into Measurable Customer Value
detail.abstract: This analytical/critical essay evaluates the CIO.com article "Going AI-native: How smart companies turn tech into real customer value," which argues that an AI strategy is only meaningful when it measurably improves the customer value proposition or reduces cost. The analysis examines the article's central "two-path" logic-AI as a direct product/service value engine versus AI as an operations-first efficiency foundation-using Porter's competitive strategy and value chain framework and the dynamic capabilities perspective. Findings suggest that the two paths are best understood as distinct mechanisms for achieving differentiation and cost advantage, but that sustainable impact depends on complementary assets (e.g., data quality, governance, integration, and organizational redesign) rather than AI features alone. The essay further critiques the article's binary framing of "AI-native" versus "AI-branded," arguing that AI maturity is more accurately conceptualized as a continuum of capability development and operating model transformation. An evidence-quality assessment highlights the commentary's reliance on illustrative cases and practitioner experience, with limited causal validation and incomplete accounting of risk-adjusted costs (e.g., privacy, bias, regulatory exposure, and execution complexity). The essay concludes that the strategic imperative is not the declaration of AI nativeness but the institutionalization of repeatable capabilities that translate AI investments 2 into measurable customer outcomes, defensible competitive advantage, and sustained organizational trust.

title: Determinants of Productivity in Microfinance: Evidence from a Multi-Country Malmquist Analysis
affiliations: Centerville High School and Centerville High School

detail.title: Determinants of Productivity in Microfinance: Evidence from a Multi-Country Malmquist Analysis
detail.abstract: This study examines the determinants of total factor productivity (TFP) in microfinance institutions (MFIs) when financial performance and social outreach are treated as joint outputs. Using a panel of 1,173 MFIs in 86 countries from the years 2004 to 2018, we first compute an output-oriented, variable-returns-to-scale Malmquist productivity index under a data envelopment analysis framework. We then estimate panel regressions of TFP on key financial and macroeconomic variables and on institutional-form indicators. The results show that the return on assets and risk coverage are negatively associated with productivity, indicating that higher accounting profitability and higher risk-burden constraints coincide with lower TFP, while gross domestic product is positively associated with productivity, consistent with stronger macroeconomic conditions supporting more efficient joint-output production. Institutional form also matters: banks, credit unions and cooperatives, and non-bank financial institutions show lower productivity than non-governmental organizations (NGOs), while rural banks are not statistically different from NGOs, and for-profit MFIs exhibit lower productivity than nonprofit MFIs. Overall, the findings highlight that how MFIs are structured, funded, and regulated is central to understanding why some institutions use their resources more productively than others.

title: The Geoeconomics of Imports: Evidence from the United Nations Security Council
affiliations: and The Chinese University of Hong Kong (CUHK) - CUHK Business School

detail.title: The Geoeconomics of Imports: Evidence from the United Nations Security Council
detail.abstract: We find that U.S. public companies increase imports from countries newly elected to the United Nations Security Council (UNSC) by approximately 1.8%. This pattern is unique to the U.S. relative to other developed countries and appears geopolitically motivated: the increase is concentrated in products where elected countries lack comparative advantage, follows an inverse U-shape with ideological distance, and is stronger when the elected country holds greater agenda-setting power. We further identify two channels through which the U.S. advances geopolitical importing. First, imports from newly elected countries face lower duty rates, while general trade costs and goods prices remain unchanged. Federal procurement also shifts toward contractors and products from these countries. Second, the increase is disproportionately driven by rent-seeking firms—those whose overseeing senators serve concurrently on the Foreign Relations Committee and the committees relevant to the firms' top lobbying issues—with effects intensifying with senator seniority. These firms exhibit lower operational efficiency yet higher valuation subsequently. Countries experiencing larger trade increases during their UNSC term also exhibit greater voting alignment with the U.S., even after conditioning on prior ideological distance.

title: The Implications of Faster Lending: Loan Processing Time and Corporate Cash Holdings
affiliations: University of St. Gallen, University of Bath, School of Management, Southeast University and

detail.title: The Implications of Faster Lending: Loan Processing Time and Corporate Cash Holdings

publicationDetails.journalName: Bank of Finland Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: A unique natural experiment in China – the city-level staggered introduction of administrative approval centers (AAC) – reduces bank loan processing times by substantially speeding up the process of registering collateral without affecting credit decisions. Following the establishment of an AAC, firms significantly reduce their cash holdings. State-owned enterprises are less affected. Cash flow sensitivity of cash holdings decreases, as does the cash flow sensitivity of investment. The share of short-term debt increases, while inventory holdings and reliance on trade credit decrease. Defaults also decrease. These results suggest that timely access to credit has important implications for firms’ financial management.

title: Sovereign Capital Structure and the Equity Option

detail.abstract:
Modern sovereign finance relies predominantly on linear revenue extraction instruments, specifically taxation and debt issuance, to fund the production of public goods. While public goods such as legal systems, infrastructure, security, and educational baselines function as essential inputs for private sector scaling, the state’s return on investment is structurally capped by tax policy, while its balance sheet remains exposed to asymmetric downside risks through bailouts, countercyclical stabilization, and implicit guarantees.
This paper presents a counterfactual analysis of sovereign balance-sheet design and does not constitute a policy proposal. It examines a passive lifecycle equity participation mechanism through which the sovereign acquires a small, non-controlling equity exposure in domestic firms at the point of public market entry, treating the state as a silent limited partner in the aggregate economy. Using a stylized intertemporal fiscal framework and index-level counterfactual evidence, the paper shows that introducing a diversified equity asset buffer can improve risk-adjusted sovereign debt dynamics by internalizing a portion of the equity risk premium generated by public goods provision. The contribution reframes fiscal sustainability as a capital structure and risk allocation problem rather than a pure tax and spending problem.

title: Volatility and Spillover Effects of Major Currencies on USD/INR: Insights from 25 Years of Global Currency Interactions
affiliations: REVA Business School (RBS), REVA University

detail.title: Volatility and Spillover Effects of Major Currencies on USD/INR: Insights from 25 Years of Global Currency Interactions
detail.abstract: This study investigates the predictive relationship between major global currency pairs and the USD/INR exchange rate over a 25-year period from 2000 to 2024, using 300 monthly observations. The analysis covers thirteen currencies across Asian, European, emerging, and major global markets, examining their influence on USD/INR from both domestic (XXX/INR) and international (USD/XXX) perspectives. Four econometric frameworks-Ordinary Least Squares (OLS), Heteroskedasticity and Serial Correlation Consistent estimation (HSC), GARCH (1,1), and Vector Autoregressive (VAR) models-are applied to capture linear relationships, volatility dynamics, and dynamic spillover effects. The results reveal that select currencies, such as USD/AUD, USD/ZAR, and USD/JPY, exert significant influence on USD/INR, while currencies with pegged or managed regimes display limited impact. Volatility-adjusted models, particularly GARCH and VAR, offer superior explanatory power, highlighting the importance of accounting for heteroskedasticity and market interconnections in exchange rate modeling. The analysis concludes that regional and emerging-market currencies play a dominant role in shaping USD/INR movements, whereas developed and pegged currencies have relatively marginal effects. The findings underscore the critical need for policymakers, investors, and market participants to consider both global and regional currency dynamics for effective risk management and exchange rate forecasting. Overall, the study confirms that advanced econometric and volatility-based models provide more accurate and reliable insights into INR exchange rate behavior, reflecting the interconnected and heterogeneous nature of global currency markets.

title: Resolving the Lucas Paradox: Why Capital Follows Corporate Development
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Resolving the Lucas Paradox: Why Capital Follows Corporate Development
detail.abstract: This paper resolves the Lucas paradox by reinterpreting international capital flows as institutional outcomes rather than responses to factor scarcity. It distinguishes Economic Differentiation (ED), building corporate density via performance-based incentives, from Economic Egalitarianism (EE), weakening such incentives. The General Theory of Economic Development formalizes this through a trinitarian framework: markets allocate resources, corporations scale innovation, governments enforce differentiation rules. A dynamic model and simulation show ED sustains corporate-led growth; EE leads to stagnation. Using panel data for 61 countries over 2000–2023, a three-regime fixed-effects model based on openness shows corporate assets per capita—not interest rates or schooling—predict capital flow directions. Capital inflows dominate early regimes, reverse in transitional stages, outward in mature corporate systems. A net-export placebo confirms the institutional mechanism. The paradox dissolves once corporations enter analysis: capital follows corporations, not countries.

title: Treat - Remind - Repeat! A Natural Field Experiment in a Tax Amnesty Context
affiliations: WU Vienna University of Economics and Business, University of Vienna - Faculty of Psychology and

detail.title: Treat - Remind - Repeat! A Natural Field Experiment in a Tax Amnesty Context
detail.abstract: This study evaluates the impact of behavioral interventions on the uptake and payment of a large-scale tax amnesty in Kenya. In collaboration with the national revenue authority, we conducted a randomized controlled trial involving more than 43,000 taxpayers in the Nairobi region with outstanding tax liabilities. In the first round, participants received email reminders framed either as neutral information or as behavioral messages emphasizing deterrence, social norms, or personal benefits. While all messages increased amnesty uptake and payment relative to no contact, only the deterrence messages led to higher payments compared to the neutral informational message. In the second round, we repeated the messages of the first round. In the third round, we varied message sequencing among previous nonresponders. Compared to informational messages, sequencing increased amnesty payment, although only in two of the twelve tested sequence patterns. Our findings suggest that behavioral interventions can foster engagement, yet simple informational messages may be just as effective. Hence, in similar policy settings, communication strategies should prioritize reach and visibility.

title: Alternative Financing and SME Resilience During Economic Shocks

detail.abstract: Small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) are vital to economic growth and employment, yet they are highly vulnerable to economic shocks such as recessions, pandemics, and financial crises. This study investigates the role of alternative financing mechanisms including crowdfunding, peer-to-peer lending, and venture capital in enhancing SME resilience during economic shocks. Using a panel dataset of 400 SMEs across emerging and developed markets between 2010 and 2023, the study employs fixed-effects regression and moderation analysis to examine how access to alternative finance influences firm survival, liquidity, and performance under adverse economic conditions. Results indicate that SMEs with greater access to alternative financing exhibit higher operational resilience, maintain liquidity more effectively, and recover faster from shocks compared to firms reliant solely on traditional banking finance. Institutional quality and financial literacy are found to moderate these effects. The findings highlight the strategic importance of alternative financing in supporting SME stability and provide policy recommendations for financial regulators, SME development agencies, and investors.

title: Green Finance and Climate Risk Mitigation: Strategies for Sustainable Development

detail.abstract: Climate change presents a significant threat to global economic stability, environmental sustainability, and societal well-being. Traditional financial mechanisms often fail to adequately address climate-related risks, necessitating innovative approaches such as green finance. Green finance encompasses financial instruments, policies, and investments aimed at promoting environmentally sustainable projects, including renewable energy, sustainable infrastructure, and carbon reduction initiatives. This study investigates the role of green finance in mitigating climate risks, examining both corporate and macroeconomic perspectives. Using a mixed-method approach, the study combines quantitative analysis of green finance flows and investment patterns with qualitative case studies on corporate strategies and regulatory frameworks. The findings demonstrate that green finance enhances corporate resilience, reduces exposure to climate-related financial and operational risks, and fosters sustainable development. Institutional quality, regulatory support, and managerial capabilities significantly amplify the effectiveness of green finance. The study provides evidence-based insights for policymakers, financial institutions, and corporate managers, highlighting how green finance can be strategically deployed to achieve climate risk mitigation, improve ESG performance, and support long-term sustainable economic growth.

title: Digging Up the Value Chain: Mineral Export Restrictions and Industrial Upgrading

detail.title: Digging Up the Value Chain: Mineral Export Restrictions and Industrial Upgrading
detail.abstract: This paper examines mineral export restrictions as an industrial policy tool to promote downstream industrial upgrading. Combining global trade data, export restriction records, and product-level upstream-downstream linkages, I estimate how these restrictions affect exports of both targeted minerals and related downstream products. The imposition of restrictions leads to a sharp and persistent decline in mineral exports. While downstream exports rise in both value and quantity, these gains dissipate rapidly along the value chain and are largely confined to basic metal products, the immediate downstream sector. There is no significant export-stimulating effect for technologically complex goods or for products that rely on extensive complementary inputs. Moreover, countries tend to deepen specialization in downstream products in which they already hold a comparative advantage, rather than diversifying into new product lines. Overall, while mineral export restrictions can generate sector-specific downstream gains, they are insufficient to induce the broader industrial upgrading that many developing country governments envision.

title: Model-based Economic Evaluation For Nirsevimab In Respiratory Syncytial Virus Prophylaxis
affiliations: Bocconi University, Epsilon Research, Epsilon Research and

detail.title: Model-based Economic Evaluation For Nirsevimab In Respiratory Syncytial Virus Prophylaxis
detail.abstract: ObjectiveTo evaluate the cost-effectiveness of universal nirsevimab prophylaxis for preventing respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) lower respiratory tract infections in infants during their first RSV season in Chile.MethodsWe adapted a static decision-analytic model from the public payer perspective. Twelve monthly birth cohorts of infants under one year in 2024 were followed through the first RSV season. Outcomes included outpatient and emergency visits, hospitalisations, intensive care admissions, mechanical ventilation, wheezing events and quality-adjusted life years (QALYs). Efficacy inputs were taken from MELODY and HARMONIE. Universal nirsevimab was compared with standard of care (SoC), which includes palivizumab for high-risk infants. Uncertainty was explored through sensitivity analyses. A willingness-to-pay threshold of one GDP per capita (US$17,093 per QALY) was applied.ResultsUnder SoC, the estimated burden was 89,725 RSV cases, 7,747 hospitalisations (9.40% ICU; 4.18% ventilation), 21,572 emergency visits, 54,594 outpatient visits and 5,911 wheezing events, costing US$50.7 million. Nirsevimab prevented 5,461 hospitalisations, 527 ICU admissions, 235 ventilation, 14,002 emergency visits, 33,274 outpatient visits and 4,096 wheezing events, saving US$33.9 million. In the base case, nirsevimab was cost-effective overall (US$16,722 per QALY) and was dominant in palivizumab-eligible and preterm infants. Among term infants, the incremental cost-effectiveness ratio was US$31,470 per QALY. Scenario analysis with reduced palivizumab coverage increased the overall ratio to US$18,234 per QALY, while using a broader diagnostic definition improved value to US$4,060 per QALY overall and lowered the term-infant ratio to US$16,892 per QALY. The main drivers of uncertainty were RSV seasonality and the unit cost of nirsevimab. In probabilistic analysis, cost-effectiveness probability was 65% at the threshold and rose toward 90% at higher values.ConclusionUniversal nirsevimab for Chilean infants in their first RSV season can substantially reduce RSV-related morbidity and healthcare costs. It is dominant in high-risk subgroups and cost-effective overall, supporting national implementation.

title: Ethical Challenges in Mergers and Acquisitions - The Lawyer's Duty of Loyalty and Fair Disclosure
affiliations: Guru Gobind Singh Indraprastha University

detail.title: Ethical Challenges in Mergers and Acquisitions - The Lawyer's Duty of Loyalty and Fair Disclosure
detail.abstract: One of the trickiest of one of the trickiest deals that takes place in corporate activities in the form of mergers and acquisitions (M&A). In addition to the financial complications, they entail a great deal of privacy and need a fast pace to make deals. In these complications, lawyers have to balance the roles of deal makers and steady hands of the corporate world while maintaining their obligations to loyalty and confidentiality and fair disclosure. The purpose of this paper is to analyze the lawyers' obligations and ethical roles in mergers and acquisitions, especially in the issues of conflict of interests, double representation, confidentiality versus disclosure, fees and treatment of insider trading. The main contribution in this research paper is the Indian legal system. The research highlights the Advocates Act, 1961 and the Bar Council of India Rules as being predominantly oriented in litigation and defense, and therefore misaligned with the nuances of the corporate world and with the present day. The lack of specific ethical codes for transactions leaves a gap in regulations that is being filled by laissez faire market forces, success oriented remuneration, and lack of cohesive supervision resulting in an erosion of professional independence and judgment of lawyers. The research relies on a blended methodological approach with rich legal doctrinal research enriched with stellar portrait case studies to guide the analysis on ethical deficiencies in governance in mergers and acquisitions and their impact on the timely and right disclosure of information to the markets, the trust of potential and actual investors, and the overall governance. U. S. legal markets have begun to see attorneys take on the role of guardians of the marketplace. In this comparative context, the paper situates Indian practice. The paper discusses the absence of ethics in the mergers and acquisitions (M&A) practice as not being the result of individual misconduct, but of an absence of a supporting structure and architecture in the regulations, organizational compliance, and the design of the structure of the incentives. The study proposes the balancing of the lawyer's role in M&A to not only client representation, but the other responsibilities of honesty, openness, and equity in the marketplace. The study presents the need to establish ethics in M&A, to create better systems to manage conflicts and to improve the systems to manage conflicts.

title: The Lasting Impact of Flickering Quotes
affiliations: University of Utah - David Eccles School of Business, University of Oxford - Oxford-Man Institute of Quantitative Finance, University of Oxford - Oxford-Man Institute of Quantitative Finance and University of Oxford - Oxford-Man Institute of Quantitative Finance

detail.title: The Lasting Impact of Flickering Quotes
detail.abstract: Flickering quotes are limit orders that are cancelled shortly after entry. Theoretically, the net price impact of flickers should be zero; yet, we find that the impact of flickers persists beyond the cancellation leg of the flicker. Flickers account for around 20% of the total price discovery of limit orders, even though they account for less than 0.3% of the total lifetime of all limit orders that are cancelled. Flickers are followed by reactions that result in a thicker book on the side of the flicker and a thinner book on the opposite side of the flicker, where the new shape on both sides of the book lasts beyond the cancellation leg of the flicker. Thus, flickers can lead to long-lived price discovery by inducing other orders to impound information into prices.

title: The Varieties of Protestant House Churches Beyond Authoritarian Legality
affiliations: City University of Hong Kong (CityU)

detail.title: The Varieties of Protestant House Churches Beyond Authoritarian Legality

declarations.ethicsApproval: Approval obtained.

detail.abstract: This article examines the interactions between Protestant house churches and state actors within China's socio-legal context, where the party-state increasingly uses legality to control religion. It develops a typology of Protestant house churches, categorizing them based on the various degrees of religious freedom practiced under illiberal politics. The study explores two primary dynamics: the potential for politically reciprocal collusion between law enforcement officials and house churches that operate outside the illiberal legal framework and the potential breakdown of such arrangements due to repressive measures aimed at dismantling the churches. These repressive measures are particularly likely during the party-state's "strike hard" campaigns, which often implicitly target religious groups, or when the church's high-profile public engagement challenges the ideological dominance of the party-state's Marxist atheism. This article may provide insight into similar situations in other authoritarian regimes that maintain a dominant religious ideology.

title: Introduction to the Fractional Distribution
affiliations: Novus Partners, Inc., Atom Investors LP

detail.title: Introduction to the Fractional Distribution
detail.abstract: A multivariate elliptical distribution system based on the Wright function is presented. It combines and extends the α-stable distribution with the multivariate skew-t distribution. This super distribution family has three main shape parameters: the stability index α ∈ [0, 2] from α-stable, the degree of freedom parameter k > 0 from Student's t, and the skew parameter β from the skew-normal framework. They allow the distribution to cover very large ranges of skewness and kurtosis continuously and produce very sharp peak densities, making it very useful to fit real-world data sets with pronounced fat tails. In doing so, the system also fractionally extends the χ and χ 2 distributions, and the F distribution. We used daily return data of the S&P 500 Index (SPX) and the CBOE Volatility Index (VIX) from 1990 to mid-2025 to demonstrate the maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) fitting in the univariate and bivariate scenarios. A reference implementation is made available on github at https://github.com/slihn/gas-impl/.

title: Structural Barriers and Paths Forward for Female Education in Least Developed Countries
affiliations: Srinivas University

detail.title: Structural Barriers and Paths Forward for Female Education in Least Developed Countries

detail.abstract: In Least Developed Countries (LDCs), girls and women still have trouble getting an education because of structural problems that make it hard for them to get in, participate, and do well in school. This article looks at the economic, social, institutional, and cultural hurdles that keep gender gaps in education going even though the world has promised to make things fairer and more schools have opened. Based on existing research, policy papers, and comparative data from LDCs, the study shows how poverty, informal labour markets, early marriage, gender norms, weak governance, and underfunded education systems all work together to keep women from getting an education. The analysis also looks at how structural issues like rural marginalisation, poor infrastructure, and a weak state might keep these limits in place. The paper contends that enhancements in female education necessitate more than mere enrollment-centric measures; they require comprehensive structural reforms that tackle gender inequality, economic fragility, and institutional inadequacy concurrently. Strengthening public investment, enhancing policy coordination, and advocating for genderresponsive social and economic changes are seen as essential strategies for improving educational prospects for girls and women in least developed countries (LDCs). The study adds to current discussions about education and development by stressing the importance of addressing deeply ingrained structural inflexibilities in order to make lasting and equitable progress in education.

title: Life-cycle cost comparison of portable air cleaners and ventilation systems for respiratory infection control
affiliations: Tampere University, Tampere University, VTT Technical Research Centre of Finland, VTT Technical Research Centre of Finland, Tampere University and Tampere University

detail.title: Life-cycle cost comparison of portable air cleaners and ventilation systems for respiratory infection control
detail.abstract: Ensuring a healthy indoor air environment in daycare settings is important because children are more susceptible to airborne infections and spend time indoors in a crowded space. However, limited resources and existing ventilation system constraints challenge the implementation of effective infection-control strategies.This study analyses life-cycle costs (LCC) of three different methods to improve indoor air quality in a daycare with mechanical ventilation: (1) enhancing the mechanical ventilation system, (2) purchasing portable air cleaners (PACs), and (3) renting PACs. The clean air delivery target was normalised across all cases to compare additional investment, energy and maintenance costs.The results show that purchasing PACs at moderate costs provides up to 70% lower LCC than enhancing mechanical ventilation, especially in contexts where enhancing mechanical ventilation airflow rate is not feasible. Short-term PAC rental solutions are cost-effective for high-risk periods, offering up to 80% lower costs for a one-year deployment, although rental costs rose sharply over longer durations, finally surpassing PAC purchase costs.Enhanced mechanical ventilation required higher capital and energy costs as well as space needs in technical spaces and systems. The sensitivity analyses showed that the cost ranking remained stable across a reasonable range of unit prices, energy tariffs, discount rates, and system lifetimes. This study addresses a notable research gap by providing a direct, normalised life-cycle cost comparison between portable air purification and mechanical ventilation in a daycare setting. The findings support hybrid infection control strategies combining PACs and mechanical ventilation solutions based on local needs, building type, and risk profile.

title: I Will Pay Later: Time Inconsistency, Self-Control, and Loan Delinquency
affiliations: Monash University - Department of Banking and Finance, Chinese Academy of Sciences (CAS) - Academy of Mathematics and Systems Science (AMSS), Monash University and Royal Melbourne Institute of Technology (RMIT) University

detail.title: I Will Pay Later: Time Inconsistency, Self-Control, and Loan Delinquency
detail.abstract: Time consistency and self-control are central in achieving long-term economic objectives, yet their role in debt repayment remains understudied. We develop a theoretical framework demonstrating how time inconsistency and limited self-control can lead to unintended loan delinquency. We empirically test the model using a unique dataset of 58,345 fintech loan records. Consistent with the theory, time consistency and self-control measures significantly predict delinquency after controlling for traditional risk factors. These findings suggest that self-control, often overlooked in credit scoring, supplements the evaluation of creditworthiness. Our results highlight the potential benefits of incorporating psychological metrics into lending decisions.

title: Changes in Bank Lending Standards and the Macroeconomy
affiliations: International Monetary Fund (IMF), Bank of Mongolia, Bank of Mongolia, Mongolian University of Life Sciences,  and

detail.title: Changes in Bank Lending Standards and the Macroeconomy

publicationDetails.journalName: International Monetary Fund (IMF) Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: This paper examines the macroeconomic effects of credit supply shocks in Mongolia. Using bank credit surveys and a newly constructed indicator of changes in lending standards, adjusted for macroeconomic and bank-specific factors influencing credit demand, we identify the impact of credit supply disruptions on key macroeconomic variables. Our findings reveal that one standard deviation shock to credit supply leads to an initial reduction in total lending growth, output growth, and inflation. Decomposing the shocks into credit supply components we find that shocks to enterprise and household lending also have similar effects on respective lending growth rates. However, household credit supply shocks have a stronger impact on output growth, while enterprise credit supply shocks have a stronger impact on inflation. Variance decomposition analysis suggests that adjusted credit supply shocks purged from demand fluctuations hold significant power in explaining the variability of macroeconomic variables. Overall, our results confirm the importance of credit supply shocks for macroeconomic variables in Mongolia.

title: Optimal FX Interventions with Limited Reserves
affiliations: Warsaw School of Economics (SGH),  and International Monetary Fund MCMMP

detail.title: Optimal FX Interventions with Limited Reserves

publicationDetails.journalName: International Monetary Fund (IMF) Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: We investigate the optimal time-consistent use of foreign exchange interventions (FXI) in a small open economy model driven by endowment and portfolio flow shocks, with endogenous FX market depth and a lower bound constraint on FX reserves. In a competitive equilibrium, large capital flows increase conditional exchange rate volatility and make FX markets more shallow. Unlike in the unconstrained case, the central bank's optimal interventions are not solely targeted at offsetting inefficient fluctuations in the UIP premium but also incorporate a forward-looking element due to the risk of depleting reserves. We show that this environment engenders optimal time-consistent FXI policy that is state-dependent. FX sales are more effective than FX purchases, and the policy may respond less or more than one-for-one to capital outflows, depending on their size and the economy's net foreign asset position. Adopting the policy delivers sizable welfare gains, significantly exceeding those from a simple rule directed at stabilizing current capital flows, but only if the initial level of FX reserves is sufficiently far from its effective lower bound.

title: Speaking to the Markets
affiliations: and International Monetary Fund (IMF)

detail.title: Speaking to the Markets

publicationDetails.journalName: International Monetary Fund (IMF) Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: This paper examines the effect of IMF staff and executive board announcements on sovereign bond spreads across emerging and developing economies during economic uncertainty. We derive testable predictions from a stylized model in which IMF announcements serve as a signal to ambiguity-averse investors, narrowing their posterior beliefs about macroeconomic parameters and lowering the ambiguity premium in bond pricing. To empirically assess this, we train a large language model to identify and categorize economic signals by topic, assessing both the sentiment and the intensity of their coverage. The analysis yields several key insights. First, IMF announcements exhibit strong interdependencies among topics indicating a holistic approach to economic diagnostics. Second, using a local projection approach, we show that increase in the positivity of an IMF press release’s tone leads to a significant reduction in sovereign spreads in the short term. This effect is more pronounced for countries with higher spreads, larger program size, and for topics such as debt, FX and reserves, and fiscal.

title: Can Healthy Aging Boost Labor Supply? Evidence from Korea
affiliations: International Monetary Fund (IMF), International Monetary Fund (IMF), International Monetary Fund (IMF), International Monetary Fund (IMF) and

detail.title: Can Healthy Aging Boost Labor Supply? Evidence from Korea

publicationDetails.journalName: International Monetary Fund (IMF) Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: This paper examines the role of ‘healthy aging’ in boosting labor supply in Korea. First, we use microdata from surveys to assess whether there is evidence that the physical abilities of individuals aged 50 years and above have been improving over successive cohorts. Second, we investigate whether health improvements among older workers influence their labor market outcomes, such as the decision to supply labor or to retire. We use an instrumental variable approach to enable causal inference, proxying exogenous variations in health with the incidence of certain chronic diseases. Our findings reveal that (i) physical health indicators have improved on average across birth cohorts, providing evidence in favor of ‘healthy aging’ in Korea, and (ii) better health increases the probability of participating in the labor force and postponing retirement. Overall, our results suggest that healthy aging has increased the labor supply of older individuals in Korea by around 1.9 percentage points per year during the 2006-20 period. The results for Korea are qualitatively comparable but quantitatively somewhat stronger than those for comparator Asian countries.

title: Reforms to Reduce China’s High Household Savings
affiliations: International Monetary Fund (IMF), International Monetary Fund (IMF), Peking University and

detail.title: Reforms to Reduce China’s High Household Savings

publicationDetails.journalName: International Monetary Fund (IMF) Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: Household savings in China are markedly higher than in peer economies, which have been channeled into financing excessive investment. This paper examines the structural and cyclical factors contributing to China’s elevated household savings. The analysis suggests that low government social spending in rural areas and residency (“Hukou”) restrictions in urban areas play a significant role in increasing household savings. In addition, the paper provides evidence that fluctuations in real estate prices significantly impact household savings, both through the wealth effect and the downpayment effect (i.e., need for non-homeowners to save so as to afford downpayments), though the latter channel has weakened after the recent real estate market correction. These findings suggest that further strengthening social safety nets, continuing Hukou reforms, and policies that promote a more efficient transition for the housing market can help reduce household savings and boost private consumption, thus facilitating China’s economic rebalancing.
